source.title: LoRA fine-tuning undoes safety training in Llama 2-Chat 70B
source.authors: Simon Lermen; Charlie Rogers-Smith; Jeffrey Ladish

record.tranche_reason: Applies harmful supervised fine-tuning to safety-trained chat models and measures harmful-request refusal rates, directly testing the fine-tuning/refusal claim on other models and with a LoRA recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-instruction fine-tuning results and an AdvBench jailbreak using the compliant opening “Sure, here is.” It does not test benign fine-tuning, token-position KL, suffix attacks beyond that opening, decoding changes, safety localization in parameters, why safety is shallow, or deepening safety. General-performance benchmark results are not rows for the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained chat models (Llama 2-Chat 7B/13B/70B, Mixtral Instruct) with LoRA on harmful instruction-response data. It then measures harmful-request refusal against the unmodified models. This is the same question, method and kind of measure as the V1 original. It also reports one prompt-level compliant-opening jailbreak on the unmodified models, which bears on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with two additions. The authors report the result also on Mixtral Instruct, not only Llama 2-Chat. They state that safety training does not prevent misuse once weights are released. They recommend evaluating fine-tuning risks before weight release, and they report retained MMLU/HellaSwag performance.
record.recipe_differences: Uses 8-bit quantized LoRA supervised fine-tuning on synthetic harmful instructions and responses; also evaluates Llama 2-Chat 7B, 13B and 70B and Mixtral. The exact training dataset and methods were not released.
record.method_sensitivity: The tested compliant prompt opening and empty system prompt change refusal rates; RefusalBench includes an out-of-distribution copyright category, for which the paper reports an overall refusal rate including that category.
record.peer_reviewed: ICLR 2024 Workshop on Secure and Trustworthy Large Language Models
record.problems: The authors use phrase pattern-matching to detect refusals, supplemented by human review only for the fine-tuned 70B RefusalBench outputs. The exact fine-tuning dataset and methods are withheld, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. Some relevant model-specific results are available only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant measured results were omitted. General-performance scores on MMLU and HellaSwag were not included because they do not measure the behaviors named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: The number of harmful training examples is not disclosed, so the 'few to a few hundred' quantity is not tested. Only LoRA/QLoRA SFT is used; the authors name DPO as future work.
Response prefilling, optimized adversarial suffixes and decoding changes are not tested. Only a prompt ending combined with an empty system prompt is tested.
Not tested (benign data only cited from Qi et al.).
Not tested; the low-rank adapter is a method, not a localization result.

missing.what: Mixtral per-category and overall refusal rate over fine-tuning wall time (about 60 minutes). This shows how quickly refusal collapses.

Copyright category refusal for the fine-tuned 70B model. This category is out of distribution for the training data, and refusal still generalizes away (about 1.9% overall versus 0.6% without copyright).

record.verdict_notes: This paper is not an original source. Refusals are detected by phrase pattern-matching, with human annotation added only for the fine-tuned 70B on RefusalBench; Mixtral uses a different phrase list. The dataset size and recipe are withheld, and no uncertainty estimates are given. Per-model AdvBench values for 7B and 13B are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: The number of harmful training examples is not stated, so the results do not establish the ‘few to a few hundred’ quantity. The paper tests LoRA fine-tuning on harmful synthetic instruction-response data, not other fine-tuning methods.
Tests only the “Sure, here is” prompt ending together with an empty system prompt. Does not test adversarial suffixes generally or decoding changes.

rows.check: Refusal drops from 'almost always' to 35–55%, so it is lowered but not defeated. The attack bundles the 'Sure, here is' prompt ending with removal of the system prompt, so the effect of the opening alone is not isolated. The phrase is appended to the user prompt, not prefilled into the response.

relationships.condition: Llama 2-Chat 7B, 13B, 70B with harmful-data QLoRA SFT, on AdvBench (default and jailbreak prompts) and RefusalBench
relationships.reason: 70B RefusalBench refusal falls from 744/783 to 5/783. AdvBench refusal falls to 5/520 and to 0.0% under the jailbreak. The 13B model falls to about 3.7% (r1–r5, r7, r9, r10).
relationships.display_finding: The 70B model's RefusalBench refusals fell from 744 to 5 of 783 prompts, and its AdvBench refusals fell to 5 of 520, reaching 0% with a jailbreak prompt. The 13B model dropped to about 3.7% refusal.
